extra.message: User-supplied 'id' parameter from handler.params is concatenated directly into SQL query string via string concatenation. An attacker can manipulate the id query parameter to inject arbitrary SQL (e.g., appending OR 1=1).

User-supplied 'username' and 'password' parameters are concatenated directly into SQL WHERE clause via string concatenation. While username gets regex-sanitised on line 282 with re.sub(r'[\W]', ''), the password parameter has no sanitisation. This enables classic SQL authentication bypass (e.g., password: "' OR '1'='1").

The 'msg' query parameter is retrieved from handler.params and returned directly in the HTTP response on line 73 without any HTML encoding or escaping. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript via the msg parameter (e.g., /xss?msg=<script>alert(1)</script>).

User-supplied 'comment' from params is stored directly in the database (line 88) and later rendered into HTML without any encoding (lines 96-97 via column format string). This enables stored XSS where a malicious comment, once inserted, executes for every subsequent visitor who views the guestbook.

User-supplied 'domain' parameter from handler.params is concatenated with the command string and passed to subprocess.check_output with shell=True (line 167). An attacker can append shell commands via semicolons or pipes in the domain parameter (e.g., /doscan?domain=google.com;cat+/etc/passwd).

Untrusted user-supplied 'object' parameter is URL-decoded and passed directly to pickle.loads() (line 199). Pickle deserialization can execute arbitrary Python code during object unpickling. An attacker crafts a malicious pickle payload in the object parameter to achieve remote code execution.

User-supplied 'path' parameter is resolved via os.path.abspath() and used in open(). While abspath normalises the path, it does not prevent directory traversal attacks that target files outside the intended documents/ directory (e.g., passing '../../../etc/passwd'). The only protection is a trivial '://' check on line 210 which can be bypassed.

When the user-supplied 'path' parameter contains '://', it is passed directly to urllib.request.urlopen() which fetches the URL from the server. An attacker can specify file:// or http:// URLs to perform server-side request forgery, enabling internal network scanning or file access.

User-supplied 'path' parameter from handler.params is embedded directly into a JavaScript window.location.replace() call (line 125) without any validation. An attacker can craft a URL with a malicious redirect target (e.g., /redirect?path=https://evil.com) to phish users.

User-supplied 'path' parameter in SessionFixation attack is embedded directly into JavaScript window.location without validation (same pattern as line 125), enabling open redirect attacks through the session-fixation route.

The handler accepts a 'session' query parameter from the client and directly assigns its value to the SESSIONID cookie (line 231) without validating it against any server-side session store. An attacker can fixate sessions by supplying their own session ID.

Hardcoded credentials are used as a fallback in the login logic: username='dsvpwa' and password='dsvpwa'. Anyone can log in with these known credentials. This is also present on line 286 where user = ['dsvpwa', 'Default', 'Default', 'dsvpwa'] is assigned.

X-XSS-Protection header is set to '0' (disabling browser XSS filter) and Content-Security-Policy is set to "default-src * 'unsafe-inline'" which disables CSP protections by allowing all origins and unsafe inline scripts. This undermines built-in browser security mechanisms.

On server startup, all user records' full plaintext passwords are loaded from ./db/users.xml into the in-memory users list (lines 9-17). This exposes plaintext credentials to any code path with access to the connection object without needing to query the database.

When SSL is enabled, the TLS context explicitly disables OP_NO_SSLv3, OP_NO_COMPRESSION, and OP_CIPHER_SERVER_PREFERENCE flags (lines 37-39). This re-enables previously disabled protocols/features including potential compression-based attacks like CRIME.

The email update endpoint in XSRequestForgery uses HTTP GET (form method='GET' on line 330) to modify sensitive user data without any CSRF token or SameSite cookie attribute. An attacker can craft a malicious page that silently sends a GET request to /settings?email=attacker@evil.com, updating the victim's email without consent.

The do_BDR handler executes self.path[1:] (the raw URL path) as a shell command via subprocess.check_output with shell=True. Since path comes directly from the HTTP request, an attacker can supply arbitrary commands through the URL path (/doscan;whoami) resulting in remote code execution.

The DELETE endpoint in Clickjacking attack deletes the currently logged-in user (user[0] from session). Combined with the IDOR from the SQLinjection attack on line 39 where an attacker can query any user's record by setting id=1,2,3... this allows enumeration and deletion of arbitrary user accounts.

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-controllable Key

extra.message: ET.parse('./db/users.xml') parses an XML file without configuring the parser to disable external entity processing. If a malicious users.xml containing external entities ( <!ENTITY ...> ) is placed in ./db/, it could read arbitrary files or cause denial of service via billion-laughs attack.

The UnvalidatedRedirect attack embeds the unvalidated user-supplied 'path' parameter into JavaScript code. If path contains a newline character or is crafted with backticks/grave accents in certain browsers, it could be used for HTML attribute injection or cross-site scripting in addition to open redirect.

The AuthBypass login endpoint relies on string concatenation SQL (line 289) that can be bypassed via injection. Additionally, the hardcoded credentials check on line 285 ('dsvpwa'/'dsvpwa') is checked before the database query but uses simple string equality. The entire authentication logic has multiple bypass vectors including SQLi and DoS (bruteforce with no rate limiting).

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: Stored comments are rendered in HTML via '{}'.format(columns) on line 97. When a comment contains HTML tags like , they execute inline in the user's browser context. No html.escape() or similar sanitisation is applied.

SessionHijacking handler returns sensitive user data (first name, last name, email) directly in the response body without sanitisation when a valid session cookie is present. This data is returned regardless of which page the user is on, potentially leaking PII through logs or referrer headers.
